title: Can AI catch AI?
subtitle: Using AI to control AI-assisted plagiarism in L2 writing
citation: Karim Ibrahim · Language Testing in Asia 16, Article 21 (2026) · doi:10.1186/s40468-026-00433-9
focus: Learn what four detector engines look for, why their performance drops, and how L2 writing teachers can use a flag as one part of an integrity decision.
notes: Five-minute talk: introduce the authorship problem, outline the four engines, show one example of a performance drop, then end with the AICEF and the principle of corroborating evidence.

qc.source: Approved Easy Paper study PDFs, checked against Ibrahim (2026), pp. 1–19.

preview: Why would a source-matching tool struggle with newly generated text?
What signals could software use to distinguish AI-generated and human writing?
What happens to detection performance when text is paraphrased?
What should an instructor do after a detector flags an L2 assignment?
What evidence would you need to compare two classifiers fairly?

map.label: The authorship problem
map.detail: Ibrahim reviews what AI-assisted plagiarism means for L2 writing assessment.

map.label: Four classifier families

deep-dive.intro: Follow the review from the classroom problem to its recommendations, with page references for each claim.

sections.title: What counts as AI-assisted plagiarism?
sections.summary: Ibrahim focuses on improper use of generative AI to complete academic assignments. Whether use is permitted matters.
points: Source matching can overlook original AI-generated wording.
One independent Turnitin study reviewed by Ibrahim caught 54.8% of the AI essays it tested.

sections.title: How was the literature assembled?
sections.summary: The critical review reports screening 57 studies and retaining 33. The author classified the studies by detection approach.
points: Searches took place in December 2024 and May 2025 across four databases and the wider web.
The review used relevance, evidence, language, dates and replicability as selection criteria. It included preprints as well as peer-reviewed work.

sections.title: Four ways to detect AI text
sections.summary: A detector is the service an instructor uses. A classifier is the mechanism behind its output.
points: Watermarking looks for a signal inserted by the generator.
Training-based classifiers learn distinctions from labeled text.
Statistical classifiers look for patterns such as predictability.
Retrieval-based classifiers look for similarity with stored output.
sections.memory: Picture one exam office with a stamp, a sniffer dog, a meter and an archive.

sections.title: Why performance changes
sections.summary: Ibrahim reports that paraphrasing reduces detection across all four approaches under studied conditions.
points: A reported watermark detection rate fell from 97% to 15% after five paraphrases.
DetectGPT fell from 70.3% to 4.6% in a different test.
These studies used different experimental setups. Compare each result with its own baseline.

sections.title: The AICEF yardstick
sections.summary: Ibrahim evaluates classifiers for reliability, generalizability and accessibility.
points: Reliability concerns accurate, robust detection.
Generalizability concerns performance across models, genres and domains.
Accessibility concerns availability and practical deployment.
sections.memory: Trust it? Take it anywhere? Afford and run it?

sections.title: The accuracy–explanation trade-off
sections.summary: The review favors fine-tuned classifiers for accuracy but notes that their reasoning can be opaque.
points: Statistical classifiers can offer more interpretable clues and show weaker performance in reviewed studies.
Ibrahim proposes an architecture that layers statistical, semantic and fine-tuned approaches.

sections.title: Using detection in class
sections.summary: A score can inform an integrity decision alongside other evidence and teacher judgment.
points: Ibrahim recommends looking at more than one detection mechanism and checking larger samples, where available.
Portfolios, discussions, interviews and process evidence can help establish what students understand and how they wrote.
The review did not independently validate named commercial products.

critique.intro: Trace the strengths and limitations of the synthesis, then decide how much weight to give the recommendations.

sections.title: Strengths of the synthesis
sections.summary: The classifier taxonomy and concrete before-and-after examples make a technical literature usable for teachers.
points: The AICEF names and defines its evaluation criteria.
The conclusion offers a proportionate classroom rule and alternatives such as portfolios.

sections.title: Fairness needs its own evidence
sections.summary: The source mentions possible bias against ESL writers, but the framework does not separately assess fairness or rate false positives for these writers.
points: A stronger evaluation would report false-positive rates on genuinely human writing across L2 groups, alongside detection rates on generated text.

sections.title: The screening trail is hard to audit
sections.summary: The review gives inclusion rules and final counts. An included-study table would clarify which earlier citations supplied background and which supplied eligible findings.
points: The paper states a 2022–2025 inclusion window but discusses earlier studies. The role of those studies is difficult to verify from the reporting.

sections.title: Performance measures and labels vary
sections.summary: The review’s comparisons span different setups and do not always use consistent descriptors.
points: Table 1 calls watermarking highly accurate, while the conclusion describes its accuracy as moderate.
A comparison table tied to metrics, datasets and conditions would make the ratings easier to interpret.

sections.title: Product examples exceed the evidence base
sections.summary: The review focuses on approaches. Named examples in the implications do not establish how well those services work in L2 classrooms.
points: Separate an architectural demonstration from independent validation of a commercial implementation.
Preprints improve coverage in a fast-moving field while introducing uncertainty about how much evidence has undergone peer review.

review-guide.intro: Use the cards for closed-book retrieval. Explain the answer out loud, then check the anchor and the Memory Link.

sections.title: Recall the four engines
sections.summary: Name each family, state what it observes, and give one limitation.
points: Watermark requires a signal from generation. Training-based models can overfit.
Statistical detectors may be less accurate. Retrieval requires an appropriate reference database.

sections.title: Explain three evaluation criteria
sections.summary: What would make an AI classifier trustworthy, portable and practical to deploy?
points: Reliability, generalizability and accessibility.
sections.memory: Trust it? Take it anywhere? Afford it?

sections.title: Interpret the numbers
points: Turnitin caught 54.8% of generated essays in one study.
A watermark measure fell from 97% to 15% after repeated paraphrasing. A DetectGPT measure fell from 70.3% to 4.6% after one paraphrase.
The changes show fragility in their separate settings.

sections.title: Apply the one rule
sections.summary: A detector flags a student’s essay. Explain what evidence could help you evaluate the flag.
points: Consult class policy and assessment conditions. Ask how the work was developed, examine process evidence, and consider what each detector actually measures.
sections.memory: Four engines, three criteria, one decision rule.

sections.title: Give a 30-second evaluation
sections.summary: The review helps teachers understand classifiers and use outputs cautiously. Its evidence would be stronger with transparent screening, comparable metrics and explicit L2 fairness measures.

quiz.question: Which classifier needs an archive of past AI outputs?
quiz.explanation: It uses similarity to content already stored in a reference collection.

quiz.question: Which set names Ibrahim’s three AICEF criteria?
quiz.explanation: The framework asks how reliably a classifier works, how broadly it transfers and how practical it is to access and run.

quiz.question: What does the reported watermark drop from 97% to 15% illustrate?
options: Robustness can fall sharply after repeated paraphrasing.
Commercial detectors always miss 85% of AI-generated essays.
Watermarking has the same accuracy across every dataset.
quiz.explanation: The figures are from a particular study and comparison.

quiz.question: What would make the review’s search easier to audit?
options: Present the biggest accuracy value from each study.
List the included studies and show how the stated eligibility rules were applied.
quiz.explanation: A clear study list would link the reported screening method to the evidence actually synthesized.

quiz.question: An L2 essay is flagged. What is the best next step?
options: Treat the score as a signal and examine writing-process evidence and context.
Make the integrity decision from the percentage alone.
Average two tools and treat the figure as proof.
quiz.explanation: Ibrahim recommends using detection as one resource alongside other evidence and judgment.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: The gain in accuracy ___ slower training.
quiz.explanation: The expression introduces what was sacrificed to obtain the gain.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: The scheme later ___ for its limitations.
quiz.explanation: This collocation describes becoming the target of strong negative evaluation.
